title: Product Name Research v2
summary: Second pass product naming research, starting from zero with full vision context.
content:
Product Name Research v2: The "Start From Zero" Edition

Steffen | 2026-03-15 For Patrik. Second pass with the full vision.

What Changed Since v1

The first round was good, but it was missing the most important thing: this product isn't just for people who already have a business. You can start a business from inside the game.

A 16-year-old opens the app with nothing but an idea. Agents help them build a real business from zero. The rooms fill up as they grow. They go from a bare room with a whiteboard to a full office buzzing with activity.

A 55-year-old CEO opens the app and finally has the team they always needed. Everything running, visible, alive.

That changes the naming completely. v1 was thinking "command center for business owners." v2 is thinking "world where a business is born."

The New Filters

Every name must pass ALL of these:

  1. Zero to empire. Works for someone with nothing AND someone with everything.
  2. Game energy. Starting feels as natural as pressing "New Game."
  3. Place, not tool. You "go to" it, not "use" it.
  4. The fun factor. "The fun way to run your business." The name itself should feel good.
  5. Universal age. Your grandma gets it. Your 16-year-old nephew thinks it's cool.
  6. App Store clean. One word. Under 3 syllables. No "AI" in the name.
  7. Verb potential. Can it become an action? "I'll ____ that."
  8. Heaven-clean. Matches the "landed in heaven" site design.
  9. No major trademark conflicts. Can't share a name with something your users would know.

What Died (and Why)

LOFT (was #1 in v1)

Dead. RealPage launched "LOFT" as a mobile app for apartment renters in early 2025. Already at 500+ properties and 3 million residents. Plus, Loft Orbital Solutions filed a LOFT trademark (serial #98566473) in the Computer & Software Services category, registered April 2025.

It was a great name. It's taken.

FORGE (new candidate, immediately killed)

Dead. Forge (withforge.com) is backed by Founders Fund and OpenAI. They're building "the next layer of human-computer interaction." That's our space. Plus: The Forge (theforgeai.com) for AI app creation, AI Forge (accelerator), Forge.AI (AI systems). The word "forge" is becoming a generic term for AI development platforms in 2026.

PLOT (new candidate, killed)

Dead. Plot Technologies (plot.so) is an active social media management platform for teams. Same SMB audience.

HAVEN (new candidate, killed)

Dead. Five separate companies: Haven (startup accounting platform, 500+ companies), Haven (mortgage, $13.7M raised), Haven (YC-backed ML platform, Berlin), IBM Digital Asset Haven, and Startup Haven (accelerator). Too crowded.

DWELL (was #4 in v1)

Dropped. Not dead (Dwell Magazine is a different category), but the word doesn't capture the "build from zero" energy. Dwell implies you're already there. The product is about BECOMING. Dwell is for the end state, not the journey.

What Survived (and Got Stronger)

KOVA

Stronger than v1. The "start from zero" context makes invented words MORE appealing, not less. When you're building something that's never existed before (a game where you build a business), the name should feel like something that never existed before.

Conflicts found: MiTek KOVA (homebuilding management software, a sub-brand of MiTek/Berkshire Hathaway). Different vertical (construction B2B), different audience, different product category. Manageable.

REALM

Much stronger. "Build your Realm from nothing" IS the product pitch. In every RPG, you start in an empty realm and build your power. Gaming DNA is even more relevant with the "start from zero" angle.

Conflicts: MongoDB Realm (developer tool). Different audience entirely.

MONDO

Unchanged. Italian for "world." "A million Mondos." Still charming. Still the "million worlds" connector.

Former Mondo (UK fintech, now Monzo) is effectively cleared.

New Candidates for v2

The "start from zero" context opens a new territory: Italian words. Italian evokes warmth, beauty, art, design, food, sunshine, premium quality. All of which match "landed in heaven." Italian words are universally approachable because most English speakers can intuit them. And they have a musicality that makes them stick.

Three of my five finalists have Italian roots. That's not a rut. That's a pattern. This product should FEEL Italian: beautiful, warm, alive, crafted with love. Not Silicon Valley cold. Not corporate clean. Mediterranean warm.

ALTO (new)

Italian for "high" or "above." The isometric view IS the alto view: you look down from above at your world. Also the musical term for the rich, warm middle voice. "Open Alto." Two syllables. Clean.

Trademark check: No major conflicts in AI/SaaS. Alto Pharmacy exists (different vertical). No direct competitors. Relatively open territory.

BRIO (new)

Italian for "spirit, vivacity, liveliness." To do something "with brio" means with enthusiasm and energy. That IS what your AI team does. They work with brio.

Trademark check: BRIO (gobrio.com) is a Salesforce consulting firm. Brio Platform is a fintech for asset managers. BrioHR exists. Briostack (pest control software). Multiple uses across industries but notably ZERO in AI/gaming/business-builder space.

The v2 Top 5

#5: BRIO

The pitch: Spirit. Energy. Life. Your AI team works with brio. Your business runs with brio.

Why it works:

  • Italian for "spirit, vivacity, liveliness." The word IS the product feeling.
  • Two syllables. Hard B opening (memorable), warm O ending (inviting).
  • "Open Brio." "Check Brio." "My Brio is buzzing."
  • The isometric rooms are ALIVE with brio. Agents moving, working, creating.
  • "Brio: The fun way to run your business." The tagline writes itself.
  • Musical, warm, premium without being pretentious.
  • A 16-year-old can say "Check my Brio" and it sounds cool.
  • A 55-year-old can say "I run everything through Brio" and it sounds sophisticated.

Why it's #5:

  • Multiple companies use "Brio" across different industries. None in our exact space, but the name isn't virgin territory.
  • BRIO is also a well-known children's wooden toy brand (trains, etc.). Some people will associate it with kids' toys. This could actually HELP (playful, creative, built to last) or HURT (childish).
  • Doesn't immediately evoke "world" or "building." It's about the ENERGY, not the PLACE.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Brio: The fun way to run your business."
  • "Brio: Where your team comes alive."
  • "Full of Brio."

#4: ALTO

The pitch: The view from above. Looking down into your isometric world. Elevated, warm, clear.

Why it works:

  • Italian for "high/above." You're literally looking at your business from the alto position. Isometric = alto view.
  • Musical connection: the alto voice is rich, warm, and the backbone of any ensemble. Your AI team is an ensemble. You're the alto holding it together.
  • Two syllables. Clean A opening, strong T in the middle, open O ending.
  • "Open Alto." "Check my Alto." "I manage everything from Alto."
  • Relatively clean trademark territory in AI/SaaS.
  • The word carries elevation without arrogance. You're above it all, but in a calm way. "Landed in heaven" energy.
  • Works in every context: "Alto for Teams." "Alto Business." "My Alto."

Why it's #4:

  • Doesn't immediately evoke "building" or "starting from zero." It's about the PERSPECTIVE, not the CREATION.
  • Alto Pharmacy is a real company (healthcare delivery). Different vertical but some name collision.
  • Some people will think of the saxophone (alto sax) or the voice type. These are positive associations but they don't connect to business/gaming.
  • Two syllables is fine but not as punchy as one-syllable options.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Alto: The view from above."
  • "Alto: A million worlds, one platform."
  • "See everything from Alto."

#3: MONDO

The pitch: Italian for "world." A million worlds, one Mondo. Direct. Fun. International.

Why it works (with v2 context):

  • "Build your Mondo from scratch." You start with an empty world and fill it.
  • "A million Mondos" = a million businesses, each one its own world. The plural works.
  • Two syllables. Hard M opening (strong), round O sounds (warm, full).
  • "Open my Mondo." "Check Mondo." "What's happening in my Mondo?"
  • Fun to say. Almost musical. Has a bounce. Rolls off the tongue.
  • Pop culture DNA: "Mondo" has been used in art (Mondo posters), film (Mondo Cane), slang ("that's mondo" = that's wild/big). All positive, all personality.
  • International flavor. Works globally. Most people intuit the meaning.
  • No major conflicts. Former Mondo (UK fintech) is now Monzo. Name is clear.

Why it's #3:

  • "Mondo" can sound slightly campy/retro. The pop culture association is a double-edged sword.
  • It means "world" literally, which is on-the-nose. The best names are one step removed from literal (Slack doesn't mean "chat," it means "ease").
  • Doesn't have the sharp, premium SOUND of the top 2. Mondo is charming. The top 2 are commanding.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Mondo: A million worlds, one platform."
  • "Build your Mondo."
  • "Welcome to your Mondo."

#2: REALM

The pitch: Your kingdom. Your domain. Build it from nothing. Rule it from above.

Why it's stronger in v2:

The "start from zero" context transforms Realm. In every RPG, you begin in an empty realm. You explore, build, recruit, grow. Your realm becomes powerful over time. The rooms fill up. The agents level up. That's EXACTLY this product.

  • One syllable. Five letters. Powerful. Immediate.
  • "Build your Realm." "Enter your Realm." "Check my Realm."
  • Gaming DNA is PURE: every gamer knows what a realm is. It's where you play. Where you rule.
  • Business DNA is equally strong: a realm is a domain of expertise, an area of control. A CEO's realm.
  • "Realm: A million worlds, one platform." The tagline snaps into place.
  • Multi-tenant is built into the word: every client gets their own realm.
  • It scales endlessly: "Realm for Teams." "Realm Business." "Realm Enterprise."
  • The word carries centuries of weight without feeling old. It's as relevant in 2026 as it was in medieval England.
  • Works for a 16-year-old: "Dude, check my Realm, I've got 6 agents running."
  • Works for a 55-year-old: "My operations are managed through Realm."

Why it's #2 and not #1:

  • MongoDB Realm exists. It's a developer database tool, completely different audience and product. But the name collision means you won't own "realm" in tech searches immediately.
  • "Realm" has been used in gaming and tech enough times that it won't produce the "why didn't I think of that" moment. It's a STRONG name, not a SURPRISING name.
  • It leans gaming-heavy. Some business users might feel it's not "serious" enough for their operations platform. (Counter-argument: the product IS a game. Lean into it.)

Tagline pairings:

  • "Realm: A million worlds, one platform."
  • "Build your Realm."
  • "Enter your Realm."
  • "Every business is a Realm."

#1: KOVA

The pitch: A word that didn't exist until you made it. Like Figma. Like Spotify. Like the product itself.

Why it's the one (with v2 context):

  1. This product has never existed before. Neither has this word. You're building the first platform where someone can start a business by playing a game. That's a new category. A new category deserves a new word. Loft, Realm, Mondo all carry existing associations. Kova carries only what you put into it. The product DEFINES Kova. Not the other way around.

  2. The "start from zero" vision IS Kova. When a 16-year-old opens the app for the first time, they have nothing. The word "Kova" has no meaning to them either. They build their business AND their understanding of the name at the same time. By the time their office is buzzing with agents, "Kova" means everything. It means THEIR business. THEIR world. THEIR team. The name grows WITH you.

  3. Finnish for "strong, powerful, hard." For those who discover the origin, it's a perfect hidden meaning. Your business makes you kova. The platform makes you kova. But 99% of users won't know this, and it doesn't matter. Figma means "articulated figure" in Japanese. Nobody knows. Nobody cares. The product gave Figma its meaning.

  4. The phonetics are elite. Hard K opening (Kodak, Kia, Kindle, Kayak, the most memorable consonant in branding). Two syllables, rhythmic, satisfying. Open A ending (warm, inviting, like "aha"). Say it out loud: "Kova." It sounds like a product you'd pay for. It sounds like something a Nike campaign would use.

  5. Completely ownable. No Founders Fund-backed competitor. No 3-million-user app. No major trademark in software. MiTek KOVA is a niche B2B construction sub-brand, and that's manageable. kova.app, getkova.com, kova.io are all reasonable domain paths. You won't be fighting anyone for mindshare.

  6. It becomes a verb naturally. "Kova it." "I'll Kova that." "Just Kova." Like "Google it" or "Slack me." The two-syllable structure with the hard K makes it snappy as an action word.

  7. It works for EVERYONE.

    • A 16-year-old: "I started my first business on Kova." (Sounds like a cool app, not homework.)
    • A 55-year-old CEO: "I run my entire operation through Kova." (Sounds premium, not childish.)
    • A developer: "We're building on the Kova platform." (Sounds technical, not fluffy.)
    • A client explaining to their friend: "It's called Kova." Done. No follow-up needed.

  8. "Landed in heaven" with an edge. The name is warm (open vowels) but sharp (hard K). That's exactly the product: a beautiful, clean, heaven-like experience with real power underneath. It's not soft. It's not corporate. It's both.

  9. App Store dominance. Nobody in AI, agent platforms, business tools, or gaming sounds like Kova. Search "Kova" right now and you get a Finnish construction software (niche) and some small agencies. By next year, "Kova" means one thing: THIS product.

  10. The "why didn't I think of that" factor comes AFTER launch, not before. With Figma, nobody said "of course" when they first heard the name. But after using the product, Figma BECAME synonymous with collaborative design. Kova will follow the same path. It's not obvious today. It's obvious in hindsight. That's the most powerful kind of name.

  11. It scales infinitely. "Kova for Teams." "Kova Business." "Kova Enterprise." "KovaOS." "Kova SDK." "Kova Marketplace." The name holds anything because it started as nothing. No box. No ceiling.

  12. The v1 concerns are actually strengths in v2. v1 said "no inherent metaphor" was a weakness. But with the "start from zero" vision, THAT IS THE METAPHOR. Both the user and the name start from zero and build meaning together. The name IS the product philosophy.

The Verdict

Kova.

A word that means nothing until you build it. Just like the business you'll start inside it.

Finnish for "strong." But you won't know that. You'll just know it's where your AI team lives. Where your business was born. Where you went from an idea to an empire.

Four letters. Two syllables. No jargon. No "AI." No corporate stiffness. No trademark conflict.

A 16-year-old builds their first thing on Kova. A 55-year-old runs their whole operation on Kova. Both feel like it was made for them.

Ship it.

Tagline Directions for Kova

  • "Kova: A million worlds, one platform."
  • "Build your Kova."
  • "Start from zero. Build everything."
  • "Where businesses are born."
  • "The fun way to run your business."
  • "Your team. Your world. Kova."
  • "From idea to empire."
  • "Open your Kova."

Runner-Up Ladder

If Kova hits trademark issues or doesn't land with Patrik:

  1. Realm (gaming DNA, build from nothing, one syllable, powerful)
  2. Mondo (Italian for world, fun, warm, direct million-worlds connection)
  3. Alto (Italian for high/above, isometric perspective, musical warmth)
  4. Brio (Italian for spirit/vivacity, the energy of the product)

Each could carry the product. But Kova is the one because it's the only name that starts from zero, just like the user.
